standfirst: Four seasons, four decades, one couple on Jeju, and a husband who is the most quietly radical thing in modern K-drama. The plot is not the point. Yang Gwan-sik is, and so is whichever grandparent this show is going to have you thinking about for a week afterwards. These seven carry some part of that.

picks.why: The closest thing to it that already existed. A neighbourhood, a decade, parents given as much interiority as their children, and the same understanding that ordinary devotion is the actual drama. Both shows make you cry hardest in a scene where nothing happens. Difference: Reply 1988 stays inside one era and one alley, so it never gives you the vertigo of watching a whole life go past.

Jeju again, and the same insistence that everyone in frame deserves a chapter. Money, mothers, illness, teenagers, and endings that are earned rather than delivered. Difference: it is an anthology, so no single marriage gets to accumulate the way Ae-sun and Gwan-sik's does across forty years.

For Gwan-sik specifically. Hwang Yong-sik is the other great K-drama man who simply decides to be on her side and never once wavers, in a town that has decided she is a problem. Difference: it is a comedy with a serial killer in it, forty short episodes rather than a stately epic. Much funnier, much less devastating.

If what got you was the ageing. Women in their seventies given a full sixteen episodes about failing bodies, adult children and old grudges, written by Noh Hee-kyung with no sentimentality anywhere. Difference: no central love story and no young timeline to cut back to. This is the hard version.

Twelve episodes about time as the antagonist, and the drama most likely to leave you in the state Tangerines did. A young woman ages fifty years and has to keep living inside it. Difference: there is a structural reveal that reframes everything, so the grief arrives as a shock rather than as accumulation.

For the historical undertow. A first romance in Gwangju in May 1980, with the period treated honestly instead of as set dressing, and two leads whose ordinariness is the whole point. Difference: twelve episodes, one era, and an ending the framing device warns you about early. Far more brutal, far less consoling.

A seventy-year-old man decides to learn ballet and a young dancer with nothing left decides to teach him. Same subject as Tangerines: what a person is still allowed to want near the end. Difference: small, tidy, twelve episodes, with none of the generational sprawl.

against.title: Crash Landing on You
against.why: Suggested because both are beloved, high-emotion and star-driven. But CLOY is a border-crossing adventure romance with a bureaucratic obstacle. Tangerines has no obstacle at all, which is precisely why it hurts. Different machinery entirely.

against.title: Mr. Sunshine
against.why: The other sweeping Korean epic with a period setting. It is grand, doomed and cinematic; Tangerines is domestic and cumulative. Go looking for Gwan-sik in Mr. Sunshine and you will find tragedy with no comfort attached.

against.title: Hi Bye, Mama!
against.why: The other great crying drama about family and mortality. It runs on a supernatural premise and a deadline, so the tears are structural. Tangerines earns them across forty years of small kindnesses, which is a harder and better trick.
